summary: Lets an IS-IS router shift traffic away from a point-to-point or LAN interface during maintenance by signaling neighbors with a higher reverse metric, the metric in the direction toward the router.

eli5.summary: Before closing a road for repairs, you put up signs telling drivers it is slow. Traffic moves away before the closure.

questions: what is the is-is reverse metric tlv
how to drain traffic from an is-is link
what is the is-is overload bit
what does the w bit do in is-is reverse metric
subtitle: A way for one IS-IS router to tell its neighbor to raise the metric toward it, so traffic drains off a link before maintenance.

tldr.problem: To take one link out of service gracefully, operators had to raise the IS-IS metric on both ends of the link at once, which is slow and error-prone, and on a LAN there was no way to steer traffic away from a single node.
tldr.mechanism: A router puts a Reverse Metric TLV (type 16) in its IS-IS Hello, carrying a metric offset that the neighbor adds to its own configured metric for that link.
tldr.outcome: Provisioning happens on one router and traffic shifts away in both directions. The RFC warns that this lets one router change a neighbor's metrics, so it strongly recommends authenticating IS-IS PDUs.

today: RFC 8500 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Drain a Link Gracefully
sections.content:
IS-IS already has the overload bit, which operators set to remove a whole router from the topology before disruptive maintenance. Routers recalculate their shortest path trees without it, so it gets no transit traffic. The RFC notes that this can push a large volume of traffic onto suboptimal paths, and that most maintenance only concerns a single link or LAN.

The older way to drain one link is to raise the IS-IS metric on both devices attached to it at the same moment. The RFC lists the problems: operators must identify the same link on two devices, configuring every device on a multi-access LAN is slow and error-prone, and there is no way to isolate just one node's interface on a LAN in both directions. Network management systems could help in theory, but the RFC says they are largely not used in service provider networks and interoperate poorly across vendors.
sections.eli5: Closing a whole town to fix one street would be silly. You only want to close the one street, and you want both ends of it to put up the sign without two people having to coordinate.

sections.title: The Reverse Metric Idea
sections.content:
The routing protocol itself carries the signal. A router adds a Reverse Metric TLV to its IS-IS Hello (IIH) PDU sent to an adjacent node on a point-to-point link or a multi-access LAN. The value is an offset: the receiver adds it to the metric it already has configured for that link, so the link becomes less attractive in the direction toward the signaling router.

Provisioning is needed on only one node, and traffic shifts away from the link in both directions. On LANs this fills a gap: IS-IS had no way to influence traffic toward one particular node.

The RFC lists other uses: a line card that is still loading forwarding entries after a reset, a spine node in a spine-leaf network pushing a higher metric to leaves when a backbone link is congested, and LDP IGP synchronization when a new node joins a LAN.
sections.eli5: Instead of two people each putting up a slow sign, one person tells the neighbor, "please treat the road to me as slower," and the neighbor does it.

sections.title: The Reverse Metric TLV
sections.content:
The TLV has type 16 and a length of 5 to 255 octets. Its value holds a 1-octet Flags field, a 3-octet Metric, a 1-octet sub-TLV length and 0 to 250 octets of sub-TLV data. It may appear in any IS-IS Hello, but a sender MUST include only one. If a receiver sees more than one, it MUST ignore all of them.

The Metric is a 24-bit unsigned offset that the neighbor SHOULD add to its configured Default Metric. In narrow metric mode the range is 0 to 63. In wide mode it is 0 to (2^24 - 2), and the value (2^24 - 1) means non-reachable.

Two flag bits are defined. The W bit (0x01, "Whole LAN") is used only on multi-access LANs and MUST be clear on point-to-point links. The U bit (0x02, "Unreachable") lets the accumulated wide metric reach (2^24 - 1), which makes the link unreachable. Reserved bits MUST be zero and are ignored on receipt.

One sub-TLV is defined, the Traffic Engineering Metric with type 18, a 24-bit offset added to the neighbor's Traffic Engineering Default Metric. If it appears more than once, the whole Reverse Metric TLV MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The message is a small note with a number and two on/off switches. The number says how much slower to treat the road, and one switch can say "treat it as closed."

sections.title: How Receivers Apply the Metric
sections.content:
Both ends of a link, and the whole area or level, should use the same metric type. The receiver adds the offset to its configured metric and caps the result at 63 in narrow mode and at (2^24 - 2) in wide mode. With the U bit set, the cap becomes (2^24 - 1). If the receiver advertises a Traffic Engineering Default Metric sub-TLV but the Reverse Metric TLV has none, it MUST NOT change that value.

For multi-topology IS-IS on point-to-point links, a router MUST send only a single Reverse Metric TLV. A receiving router MUST add the metric to its Default Metric in all Extended IS Reachability TLVs for all topologies.

On a LAN, only the Designated Intermediate System (DIS) SHOULD act on the TLV, and all other nodes MUST silently ignore it. With the W bit clear, the DIS adds the metric to the Pseudonode LSP entry for just the sending node. With the W bit set, the DIS adds it for every node on the LAN, using the reverse metric from the non-DIS with the highest source MAC address that set W. Local provisioning on the DIS takes precedence over received TLVs.
sections.eli5: Each neighbor adds the extra cost to the sign it already has, but never beyond a maximum. On a shared street, the person in charge of the signs decides whether the extra cost applies to one driveway or the whole street.

sections.title: LDP Synchronization and Operations
sections.content:
RFC 6138 addresses LDP IGP synchronization on broadcast networks. With Reverse Metric, a new node joining a LAN can, besides setting the maximum link metric (2^24 - 2) per RFC 5443, SHOULD also advertise the maximum metric offset in its Hello. It continues until LDP label exchanges finish with all neighbors on the LAN, either through the LDP End-of-LIB signal or a provisioned timeout. Other nodes on the LAN are not affected.

Operational guidance: advertise the TLV only for the duration of the maintenance window. It does not change metrics stored in the router's persistent configuration. A syslog message or SNMP trap on receipt helps find the node advertising a changed metric. When a Traffic Engineering metric reaches (2^24 - 1), the router SHOULD trigger an immediate CSPF recalculation. Implementations should let operators disable acceptance of Reverse Metric, and if it is on by default, operators are RECOMMENDED to turn it off when not using it.
sections.eli5: A new house on the street can say "send no traffic to me yet" until its water and power are ready, without making the rest of the street slower.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The mechanism lets one IS-IS router manipulate the Default Metric and optionally Traffic Engineering parameters of adjacent neighbors. IS-IS routers in one autonomous system are nearly always under a single administrator, but the RFC says it is highly recommended to configure authentication of IS-IS PDUs so the TLV cannot be used as an attack vector.

IANA allocated IS-IS TLV codepoint 16 for the Reverse Metric TLV, valid in IIH PDUs only. The RFC also creates the registry "Sub-TLVs for TLV 16 (Reverse Metric TLV)" with Expert Review policy. Value 0 is reserved, 18 is the Traffic Engineering Metric, and the rest are unassigned.
sections.eli5: Because a neighbor can now change your road signs, you should check that the note really came from a trusted neighbor.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved bits, then U (0x02) and W (0x01).

fields.name: Metric
fields.desc: Metric offset added to the neighbor's configured metric.

items.label: W bit
items.desc: Whole LAN: DIS applies the metric to every node. Clear on point-to-point links.

items.desc: Unreachable: accumulated wide metric may reach 2^24 - 1.
